Statuspage supports several ways to update component status automatically, and it can also display system metrics.

- **Email:** Components can be updated by sending an email whose subject line includes "UP" or "DOWN" (automatically update the status of components by triggering an email). Atlassian also describes email automation and the API as the main ways to pull component data (Email automation and the API are some of the main ways to pull component data).
- **Monitoring tools:** Atlassian lists DataDog, New Relic, Librato or Pingdom as monitoring integrations that can update the page when an issue is detected. Datadog's documentation says you can update the status of your systems with Datadog monitor notifications, using a component-specific email address.
- **Alerting tools:** Integrations with Opsgenie, PagerDuty, VictorOps, or xMatters let you change status from the alerting app.
- **Custom API:** The REST API lets you write your own integration (Create your own Statuspage integration using our powerful API.). Postman's integration shows this in practice: a linked monitor can change a component's status when a test run fails (When the specified monitor fails a test run, it changes the status of the linked component.).
- **System metrics:** Pages can connect to your monitoring tool to display metrics right on your page, and custom metrics can be added through the API (You can also create custom metrics through our API.). Atlassian's support docs cover metric setup for Pingdom, New Relic, Datadog, and Librato.

The search turned up no details on plan requirements or current limits for these features, so check Atlassian's current documentation before relying on specifics.

The search returned only Events API v2 material. Nothing on public status pages or business services came back, so that half of the query is unanswered.

**Events API v2 basics:**
- Monitoring tools push events to PagerDuty, and each event can mark an incident as triggered, updated, or resolved. PagerDuty's Events API V2 lets you push events from your monitoring systems to PagerDuty. You can push such events when an incident is triggered, updated, or resolved.
- Setup is done per service. You add an Events API v2 integration under the service's Integrations tab and copy the integration key, which the API calls the routing key. In PagerDuty, open the service, then Integrations, click Add an integration and pick Events API V2. Copy its Integration Key: the Events API calls it the routing key.
- Follow-up events must reuse the same deduplication key. When your system sends an update, or a resolved event, the DEDUP_KEY must match the one sent during the trigger call.
- Events need certain fields. One vendor guide notes that an event without a summary, a source or a severity is refused too.
- Severity accepts critical, error, warning, or info.

**Examples of tools that use it:** Coroot, Mackerel, Courier, and OneUptime each document a setup that uses an Events API v2 key. Mackerel also notes that by default, when an alert is closed in Mackerel, the incident will also close in PagerDuty.

**Not covered:** Nothing about PagerDuty public status pages or business services came back. A follow-up search on those topics would be needed.

The official PagerDuty docs describe the External Status Page as a public-facing view of infrastructure health, built from business services. Two versions of the page give different plan details, so check current pricing with PagerDuty's sales team.

- **Purpose and customization:** The page gives outside audiences one place to check infrastructure health. Teams can brand it and choose which sets of business services appear in each view (support.pagerduty.com/docs/external-status-page).
- **Subscribers:** Visitors can follow ongoing incidents and subscribe for email notifications. A separate version of the page also lists Slack and webhook delivery (support.pagerduty.com/main/docs/external-status-page).
- **Subscriber caps:** The newer version lists 250 subscribers for Professional, 500 for Business, and 1,000 for Enterprise (support.pagerduty.com/main/docs/external-status-page).
- **Plan conflict:** The older version calls the feature an add-on that must pair with an Incident Response or Customer Service plan (support.pagerduty.com/docs/external-status-page). The newer version says it is available on all plans, with extra pages or subscribers available as an add-on (support.pagerduty.com/main/docs/external-status-page).
- **Limits:** A business service can be attached to a status page up to a limit of 500, and an account can hold up to 100 status pages (support.pagerduty.com/main/docs/external-status-page).

# Pulse: competitive research

**Legend:** ✅ **Verified**: found in the vendor's docs or product pages during this research (sources at the end) · ⚠️ **Partial or unconfirmed**: secondary source only, or the docs conflict · 💡 **Recommendation**: my opinion for Pulse

I only list capabilities I found evidence for. Where my searches found nothing, I say so rather than fill the gap from memory.

---

## 1. Atlassian Statuspage

| Question | Findings |
|---|---|
| **Purpose / users** | ✅ A status communication product. Companies use it to tell customers and internal users about incidents and maintenance. It is **not a monitor**: it doesn't check services itself. |
| **Health monitoring** | ✅ None built in. Component status changes by hand, by email automation (subject line containing "UP" or "DOWN"), through the REST API, or through integrations: monitoring tools (Datadog, New Relic, Librato, Pingdom) and alerting tools (PagerDuty, Opsgenie, VictorOps, xMatters). |
| **Incidents** | ✅ A four-stage public lifecycle: **Investigating → Identified → Monitoring → Resolved**. Each update is timestamped and lists the affected components. |
| **Customer communication** | ✅ Component levels: **Operational, Degraded Performance, Partial Outage, Major Outage, Maintenance**. ✅ Subscribers get email for every update. SMS (paid plans only) goes out only on create, resolve and maintenance start. ✅ Sign-ups are protected by reCAPTCHA and rate-limited. |
| **Metrics** | ✅ "System metrics" can display data from Datadog, New Relic, Pingdom or Librato, or custom metrics posted through the API. ⚠️ I couldn't confirm the 90-day uptime bar from Atlassian's docs (it's widely seen but unverified here). |
| **Relevant to Pulse** | The five-level component vocabulary, the separation between internal state and public message, and the timestamped public update timeline. |

## 2. PagerDuty

| Question | Findings |
|---|---|
| **Purpose / users** | ✅ Incident response and on-call alerting for engineering and operations teams. |
| **Health monitoring** | ✅ Mostly **ingests events** from other tools through Events API v2 (trigger, acknowledge, resolve). Each event needs a summary, source and severity (critical, error, warning or info). ⚠️ I didn't verify whether it has native synthetic checks. |
| **Incidents** | ✅ Statuses **Triggered → Acknowledged → Resolved**. ✅ **Dedup key**: a trigger with the same key as an open incident is appended to it, not opened as a new incident. ✅ Acknowledge events for resolved or unknown incidents are **discarded**. ✅ Escalation policies, and acknowledging stops escalation. ✅ By default, notifications fire on trigger, not on ack or resolve. ⚠️ Intelligent alert grouping exists but I didn't verify how it works. |
| **Customer communication** | ✅ External Status Page built from "business services", with branding and email subscribers. Some doc versions also list Slack and webhooks. ⚠️ Plan availability differs between doc versions. ✅ A separate internal status dashboard exists. |
| **Metrics** | ✅ **MTTA** = average time from incident creation to first ack (unacknowledged incidents excluded). **MTTR** = creation to resolve (unresolved excluded). ✅ "Interruptions" counts responder notifications, with several channels to the same person counted once. |
| **Relevant to Pulse** | Dedup (one open incident per service), rejecting ack after resolve, exact MTTA/MTTR definitions, and the clear trigger/ack/resolve state machine. |

## 3. Better Stack (Uptime)

| Question | Findings |
|---|---|
| **Purpose / users** | ✅ Uptime monitoring, on-call and incident management, and status pages in one product, aimed at engineering teams. |
| **Health monitoring** | ✅ Active checks with a request timeout. ✅ The check frequency must not be shorter than the request timeout (the configuration is rejected otherwise). |
| **Incidents** | ✅ **Confirmation period**: wait after a failure before opening an incident ("immediate" is an option). ✅ **Recovery period**: the service must stay up for a set time before the incident resolves. Their example is 30-second checks with a 1-minute recovery, which needs 2 consecutive successes, and **any failure resets the countdown**. ✅ Tiered escalation (for example, Tier 1 → Tier 2 after 15 minutes without ack). Ack stops escalation. ✅ An "I'm unavailable" option passes the incident to the next person. |
| **Customer communication** | ✅ Built-in status page, email subscriptions, embedded response-time charts. ✅ Webhook subscriptions to status updates exist (docs page found). |
| **Metrics** | ⚠️ Response-time charts confirmed. SLA or availability reporting not verified in this research. |
| **Relevant to Pulse** | **The confirmation and recovery periods are the most directly useful idea for Pulse.** They solve the flaky and blip cases in the drill. The timeout ≤ interval validation also applies. |

## 4. UptimeRobot

| Question | Findings |
|---|---|
| **Purpose / users** | ✅ Simple website and service uptime monitoring, popular with small teams (it has a free tier). |
| **Health monitoring** | ✅ Monitor types: HTTP(S), Keyword, Ping, Port, DNS, Heartbeat (cron and background jobs), SSL. ⚠️ Fastest interval is reported as 15s or 30s depending on the page. Free plan is 5 minutes. ✅ A failed check is **re-run from a second location before alerting**. |
| **Incidents** | ✅ Logs downtime incidents with timestamps. Alerts by email, SMS, call and other channels, with escalation rules. ⚠️ I found no evidence of an acknowledge/notes workflow, so I'm not claiming one. |
| **Customer communication** | ✅ Status pages built from chosen monitors or tags. Optional custom domain, password protection, and incident or maintenance announcements that visitors can subscribe to by email. |
| **Metrics** | ✅ Uptime % and a response-time chart. ⚠️ A third-party guide describes 24h/7d/30d/90d uptime windows and avg/min/max response time on status pages. ✅ The generic formula on UptimeRobot's site is (total time − downtime) / total time × 100. Their exact computation is unconfirmed. |
| **Relevant to Pulse** | Multiple uptime windows (24h/7d/30d), "confirm before alerting" (Pulse can't use a second location, but it can retry), and the simple layout. |

---

## Comparison table

| Capability | Statuspage | PagerDuty | Better Stack | UptimeRobot | **Pulse (proposed)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Active health checks | ❌ (integrations) | ⚠️ mainly ingests events | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ HTTP, own schedule per service |
| Anti-flap rule | n/a | ✅ dedup key | ✅ confirmation + recovery periods | ✅ second-location re-check | 💡 N failures to open, M successes to close |
| Incident lifecycle | Investigating / Identified / Monitoring / Resolved | Triggered / Ack / Resolved | Open / Ack / Resolved + escalation | Down / up log | 💡 Open / Acknowledged / Resolved + notes |
| Escalation / on-call | via integrations | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ rules | ❌ out of scope |
| Public status page | ✅ core product | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ must-have #7 |
| Status levels | 5 levels | n/a | n/a (verified) | up / down | 💡 Healthy / Degraded / Down |
| Subscribers | email, SMS | email (+ Slack/webhook ⚠️) | email, webhook | email | ❌ stretch goal |
| Uptime / SLO | ⚠️ | ❌ (not its focus) | ⚠️ | ✅ uptime % | ✅ must-have #5: against target + error budget |
| MTTA / MTTR | ❌ | ✅ | ⚠️ | ❌ | ✅ must-have #9 (+ MTTD, checker health) |
| Webhook notifications | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ open + resolve (must-have #8) |

**Where Pulse is different** 💡: No single product I researched is both the monitor and the system that tracks reliability against a per-service target with an error budget. Pulse covers both ends: detection and public status, plus SLO accounting. That combination is the story for your demo.

---

## Five product design ideas to borrow 💡

1. **Confirmation and recovery thresholds** (from Better Stack). Open an incident after N consecutive failures and close it after M consecutive successes; any failure resets the recovery count. This is the single defence against the drill's `flaky 50%` step and against one-off blips.
2. **One open incident per service** (from PagerDuty's dedup key). The service ID is the dedup key. New failures attach to the open incident's timeline. Reject ack or notes on resolved incidents, as PagerDuty discards those events.
3. **Separate internal state from the public message** (from Statuspage). Pulse stores raw errors for operators, but the public page shows only a fixed, friendly mapping such as "Payments: Degraded performance". This deals with the `10.12.4.7` trap by design, not by filtering.
4. **Exact metric definitions** (from PagerDuty). MTTA = created → first ack. MTTR = created → resolved. Exclude open incidents. Add **MTTD** = first failed check → incident opened, which Pulse can measure precisely because it runs the checks.
5. **Validate configuration up front** (from Better Stack). Reject a timeout ≥ interval and an SLO target outside (0, 100]. A bad configuration gives misleading health data, and validation is cheap to test.

## Three features to avoid in six hours 💡

1. **On-call schedules and escalation policies.** These are the core of PagerDuty and Better Stack, but they're a product in themselves (rotations, tiers, timeouts). A simple "acknowledged by" field covers the must-have.
2. **Customer subscriptions (email/SMS).** These need delivery, unsubscribe and abuse protection (Statuspage uses reCAPTCHA and rate limits). They're listed as "going further", not a must-have.
3. **Multiple check types and multi-region checks** (Ping, DNS, SSL, Heartbeat, second-location confirmation). The kit only exposes HTTP `/health`. Retrying before marking a failure gets most of the benefit.

*(Also skip Statuspage's four-stage public lifecycle and the five status levels. Three levels plus open/ack/resolved is enough and easier to test.)*

## Ways to make Pulse useful without overengineering 💡

- **Plain-language public status messages**, from a fixed mapping per state. No free text from operators goes public.
- **"Since" timestamps everywhere**, such as "Down since 14:02 (6 min)". Cheap, and the first question both support and engineers ask.
- **Error budget in minutes**, for example "21.6 of 43.2 min left this window". Engineers grasp minutes faster than percentages.
- **Uptime for 24h / 7d / 30d** (UptimeRobot-style) next to the target. Gives you a short window for the demo and a real one for credibility.
- **Self-monitoring as a metric**: scheduler lag and check success rate. Covers must-have #9's "how the checking itself is performing", and it's how you'd catch Pulse failing silently.
- **Webhook payload useful at a glance**: service, owner, state, started_at, duration on resolve, and a dashboard link. Send each event exactly once and record every send attempt.
- **Show the active rule on screen**, such as "Down = 3 failures in a row". It makes the demo explainable and makes the live "change the threshold" request trivial.

---

### Research gaps
- I couldn't verify how UptimeRobot computes its 90-day uptime, Better Stack's SLA reporting, or how PagerDuty's alert grouping works. None of these changes the recommendations above.
- PagerDuty's docs conflict on which plans include the status page.

**Next step:** Use the Better Stack and PagerDuty findings to fix your state rules (N failures, M successes, timeout below 3 seconds or not) before writing `PLAN.md`. Those rules decide how the drill behaves.

The search returned mostly git commit diffs from Uptime Kuma mirrors and one borgmatic docs commit, not official documentation. Those diffs still give a useful picture of how these settings work.

- **Retry interval:** It was added so a failing check can be repeated faster, which helps you notice when a site comes back. If a check fails and retries are used you can now specify a specific value for that. So you can check faster if the site goes back up again.
- **Retries and pending:** Retries delay the down state. The retries setting is described as the maximum retries before the service is marked as down and a notification is sent. A borgmatic example shows the arithmetic: with Retries set to 6 and a retry interval of 360 seconds, the monitor goes into the "Pending" state for a grace period of about 10 minutes before a missed heartbeat is logged.
- **Retry interval logic conflicts across sources:** One diff says the retry interval is used only when it is greater than zero. A later commit changes the check to use it whenever it differs from the normal interval. The later code is the more recent behavior, but I didn't confirm which version you run.
- **Resend notifications:** The borgmatic docs describe a setting for resending notifications while a monitor keeps failing, with the example Resend Notification every X times = 1. The Uptime Kuma UI shows "Resend every X times" or "Resend disabled" labels in its translation files.
- **Upside-down mode:** This flips the result. The translation text says that if the service is reachable, it is DOWN.
- **Notification behavior during pending:** One diff shows that pending beats don't trigger an "important" status-change notification, and that a recovery from pending to up doesn't notify.

For authoritative details, check the official Uptime Kuma documentation or the current source on GitHub, since these results are from older and mirrored commits.

content.text:
# Pulse: how four products handle the five topics

**Legend:** ✅ Verified (vendor docs, or the project's own source for Uptime Kuma) · ⚠️ Secondary source or conflicting info · ❓ Not found in my research, so I make no claim · 💡 My recommendation

The four products split into two groups:
- **Monitors:** Uptime Kuma and Better Stack actively check services.
- **Responders/communicators:** PagerDuty and Statuspage react to signals from other tools.

Pulse has to be both.

## Comparison

| Topic | Atlassian Statuspage | Uptime Kuma (self-hosted, open source) | Better Stack | PagerDuty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Health check rules** | ✅ **No checks of its own.** Status changes by hand, by email ("UP"/"DOWN" subject), through the API, or from Datadog, New Relic, Pingdom or PagerDuty. | ✅ Active checks per monitor with their own interval. ✅ "Upside-down mode" inverts the result. | ✅ Active checks with a request timeout. ✅ **The interval may not be shorter than the timeout** (the configuration is rejected). | ✅ Mainly **receives events** from monitoring tools (Events API v2: summary, source, severity). ❓ Native checks not verified. |
| **Avoiding flapping** | n/a. The quality of input is up to whatever updates it. | ✅ **Retries**: after a failure the monitor goes **"Pending"** and retries before marking "Down". ✅ A separate (shorter) **retry interval**. ⚠️ Pending→Up sends no notification (from source commits). | ✅ **Confirmation period** before opening an incident. ✅ **Recovery period** before resolving. **Any failure resets the recovery countdown.** | ✅ **Dedup key**: events for an already-open incident are appended to it, not opened as new incidents. |
| **Incident lifecycle** | ✅ Public stages: **Investigating → Identified → Monitoring → Resolved**, timestamped, with affected components. | ✅ Manual incident banners on the status page (create, update, resolve). ✅ Maintenance windows (one-time or recurring) suppress false alerts. ❓ No acknowledge workflow found. | ✅ Open → **Acknowledged** → Resolved. ✅ Ack stops escalation. ✅ Tiered escalation. | ✅ **Triggered → Acknowledged → Resolved**. ✅ Ack stops escalation. ✅ **Ack on resolved or unknown incidents is discarded.** ✅ By default, alerts fire on trigger only. |
| **Public status page** | ✅ Its core product. Five levels: **Operational, Degraded Performance, Partial Outage, Major Outage, Maintenance**. ✅ Email subscribers. SMS on paid plans, and only for create, resolve and maintenance start. | ✅ No login needed to view. ⚠️ **No visitor subscriptions** (third-party guide). ⚠️ Per-monitor uptime history and response-time graph. | ✅ Built in. ✅ Email and webhook subscribers. ✅ Embedded response-time charts. | ✅ External status page built from "business services", with email subscribers. ⚠️ Plan availability conflicts between doc versions. |
| **SLO / error budget** | ❓ Not found. ✅ Can display "system metrics" pulled from monitoring tools. | ⚠️ Uptime % and history only. ❓ No targets or budgets found. | ❓ Not verified. | ✅ **MTTA** (created → first ack) and **MTTR** (created → resolved), with open incidents excluded. ❓ No native SLO found. |

**Key finding** 💡: None of the four products clearly offers **per-service targets with an error budget** in what I could verify. Tools like Datadog do (✅ Datadog docs describe error budget alerts). Pulse's must-have #5 is therefore a real point of difference, so build it carefully and highlight it in the demo.

Reference arithmetic (✅ isdown.app): a 99.9% target over 30 days = **43.2 minutes** of allowed downtime.

---

## Eight ideas to copy 💡

1. **A "Pending" state between Healthy and Down** (Uptime Kuma). The first failure → *pending* (internal only, no incident). N consecutive failures → *down* and an incident opens. One blip never pages anyone.
2. **A recovery streak that resets on any failure** (Better Stack). The incident closes only after M consecutive successes. This handles the drill's `flaky 50%` step: quotes won't open and close an incident every few seconds.
3. **One open incident per service** (PagerDuty dedup). The service ID is the dedup key. New failures attach to the existing incident's timeline instead of opening duplicates. This is easy to unit-test.
4. **Reject invalid transitions** (PagerDuty). Acknowledging or adding notes to a resolved incident returns 409. Keeping the state machine strict makes the timeline trustworthy.
5. **Notify only on open and resolve** (PagerDuty default, Statuspage SMS rule). Exactly the two webhook events the must-have asks for. Ack and notes appear in the timeline but don't notify, which avoids noise.
6. **Timeout must be less than the interval** (Better Stack). Validate it in the catalogue API. It also makes your scheduler-isolation argument clean: a check can never overlap the next one for the same service.
7. **A fixed vocabulary for the public page** (Statuspage). Map internal states to customer wording: Healthy → "Operational", Degraded → "Degraded performance", Down → "Major outage". The public page renders **only** these strings and timestamps, never stored error text, so the `10.12.4.7` leak can't happen.
8. **Exact metric definitions** (PagerDuty), plus **MTTD**. Write down MTTA/MTTR exactly as PagerDuty defines them, excluding open incidents, and add MTTD = first failed check → incident opened. Pulse can measure that precisely because it runs the checks.

## Three to deliberately skip 💡

1. **Escalation policies and on-call rotations** (PagerDuty, Better Stack). These are a whole product: tiers, timeouts, schedules. A single "acknowledged by" field covers the must-have.
2. **Statuspage's four-stage public lifecycle and five status levels.** Investigating/Identified/Monitoring needs a person writing public updates, and Partial vs Major Outage needs component modelling. Three states plus open/ack/resolved is enough and fully testable.
3. **Status page subscriptions and maintenance windows** (Statuspage, Better Stack, Uptime Kuma). Subscriptions need delivery, unsubscribe and abuse protection (Statuspage uses reCAPTCHA and rate limits). Maintenance windows would change your SLO maths. Both are "going further" items. Log them in `DECISIONS.md` as deliberate cuts.

---

### Decisions this research should feed into (yours to make)
- Failures needed to go Down (N), and successes needed to recover (M).
- Health check timeout. **If it's under 3 seconds, the drill's slow payments shows as Down, not Degraded.**
- Whether Degraded counts against the SLO, and whether to measure availability by check count or by time.

### Research gaps
- Uptime Kuma details came from mirrored source commits and third-party guides, not official docs.
- I found no native SLO feature for Statuspage, Better Stack or PagerDuty. That's an absence of evidence, so phrase it that way in `PLAN.md`.

Sources:
- [Statuspage – Integrations](https://www.atlassian.com/software/statuspage/integrations)
- [Statuspage – Enable subscribers](https://support.atlassian.com/statuspage/docs/enable-subscribers/)
- [Statuspage – System metrics](https://support.atlassian.com/statuspage/docs/show-real-time-performance-with-system-metrics)
- [Atlassian Guard status page (component levels)](https://guard.status.atlassian.com)
- [Metastatuspage incident example](https://metastatuspage.com/incidents/n141hfm11db9)
- [Uptime Kuma – retry interval commit](https://git.hackliberty.org/Infra-Mirrors/uptime-kuma/commit/f8f9f59464ab8fcc6bf57b159d51f2660b74152c)
- [Uptime Kuma – commit (pending/notification logic)](https://git.hackliberty.org/Infra-Mirrors/uptime-kuma/commit/72783fd94c0dc0583c2ade12ad026d5e396ad75d)
- [borgmatic docs – Uptime Kuma retries/pending example](https://projects.torsion.org/borgmatic-collective/borgmatic/commit/3e6004363237534400636641fbe036851af34a43)
- [Uptime Kuma status pages guide](https://selfhosted-sh.pages.dev/uptime-kuma-status-pages)
- [Uptime Kuma incidents & maintenance guide](https://www.dchost.com/blog/en/?p=4701)
- [Better Stack – Confirmation and recovery period](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/confirmation-and-recovery-period/)
- [Better Stack – Request timeout](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/request-timeout/)
- [Better Stack – On-call](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/getting-started-with-oncall-v2/)
- [Better Stack – Webhook subscriptions](https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/status-pages/subscribing-to-status-updates/subscribing-with-webhooks/)
- [Better Stack – Incident management](https://betterstack.com/incident-management)
- [PagerDuty – Incidents](https://support.pagerduty.com/docs/incidents)
- [PagerDuty – Analytics Dashboard](https://support.pagerduty.com/docs/analytics-dashboard)
- [PagerDuty – External Status Page](https://support.pagerduty.com/main/docs/external-status-page)
- [Ansible pagerduty_alert (dedup behaviour)](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/community/general/pagerduty_alert_module.html)
- [Datadog – Error budget](https://docs.datadoghq.com/service_management/service_level_objectives/error_budget/)
- [isdown.app – Error budgets](https://isdown.app/blog/error-budget-sre)

# Pulse – Plan (Gate 1)

> Legend: **✅ Decided** · **⏳ TBD**: open, must be resolved before or while building · **💡 Proposal**: awaiting my confirmation

---

## 1. Problem in my words

Acko runs many services. When one fails or slows down, nobody finds out in time:

| User | Pain today | Outcome they need |
|---|---|---|
| **On-call engineers** (service owners) | Hear about failures late, often from support | Get alerted fast, with one incident per outage, a timeline, and the ability to acknowledge and add notes |
| **Support team** | Customers call and support has no context | See at a glance what is broken and since when |
| **Customers** | Payment fails or claim is stuck: "is it me or Acko?" | A public status page in plain language, with no internal details |
| **Leads** (secondary) | Can't say how reliable a service really was | Availability against target, and the error budget left |

**The outcome that matters:** detect problems quickly (low MTTD), don't cry wolf (no flapping or duplicate incidents), and keep everyone informed until recovery.

---

## 2. Product owner Q&A

| # | Question | PO answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How frequently should Pulse check each service? | ⏳ *awaiting answer* |
| 2 | What timeout should classify a service as slow or unhealthy? | ⏳ |
| 3 | Should one failed check create an incident, or multiple consecutive failures? | ⏳ |
| 4 | How many successful checks before resolving an incident? | ⏳ |
| 5 | What conditions classify degraded rather than down? | ⏳ |
| 6 | Can multiple incidents be open for the same service? | ⏳ |
| 7 | What exact payload and endpoint does the webhook receiver expect? | ⏳ |
| 8 | Should customers see detailed error messages or only service status? | ⏳ |
| 9 | What observation window for availability? | ⏳ |
| 10 | Which features matter most if I can't finish everything? | ⏳ |
| 11 | Should historical check data survive restarts? | ⏳ |
| 12 | Is authentication required for the operator dashboard? | ⏳ |

*Answers to be copied word for word. Where the PO says "your call", the decision goes in DECISIONS.md.*

---

## 3. Research findings (Statuspage, Uptime Kuma, Better Stack, PagerDuty, UptimeRobot)

- **Anti-flapping is standard.** Uptime Kuma uses retries and a "Pending" state before "Down". Better Stack uses a confirmation period before opening and a recovery period before resolving, and any failure resets recovery. → Supports my "3 failures in a row" and "2 successes in a row" rules.
- **Dedup.** In PagerDuty, an event for an already-open incident is appended to it, not opened as a new incident. Ack events for resolved incidents are discarded.
- **Lifecycle.** PagerDuty and Better Stack use Triggered/Open → Acknowledged → Resolved. Acknowledging stops escalation.
- **Notifications.** PagerDuty notifies on trigger by default. Statuspage SMS goes out only on create and resolve.
- **Public page.** Statuspage separates component status (Operational / Degraded Performance / Partial Outage / Major Outage / Maintenance) from internal detail.
- **Config validation.** Better Stack rejects a check interval shorter than the request timeout.
- **Metrics.** PagerDuty: MTTA = created → first ack; MTTR = created → resolved; open incidents are excluded.
- **SLO / error budget.** I found no native per-service SLO with error budget in the four tools I verified. Datadog has one. This is where Pulse adds value. Reference: 99.9% over 30 days = 43.2 min of budget.

---

## 4. Decisions so far

| Area | Decision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Stack | Python **FastAPI** + **SQLite** + **httpx** (async) + server-rendered HTML (Jinja2) + **pytest** | ✅ |
| Down rule | **3 failed checks in a row, or timeout** | ✅ (see open Q-A, Q-B) |
| Degraded rule | **Response > 1000 ms, or failure ratio > X in last N checks** | ✅ shape / ⏳ X and N |
| Recovery rule | **2 successful checks in a row** | ✅ (see open Q-D) |
| Incident opens on | **Down + Degraded** | ✅ (see open Q-E, Q-F) |
| SLO window | **Rolling 30 days**, plus a **1-hour view** for the demo | ✅ |
| Degraded counts as | ⏳ **up or down** in the availability calculation | ⏳ |
| Out of scope | ⏳ see §5 | ⏳ |

### Open questions arising from my rules (must be resolved)

- **Q-A. "Or timeout".** Does a **single** timeout mark the service Down immediately, or does a timeout count as **one failure** towards the 3-in-a-row?
- **Q-B. Timeout value.** Not decided. This matters for the drill: payments is set to `slow 3000ms` and **still returns 200**.
  - If timeout < 3000 ms → payments is treated as **Down**.
  - If timeout > 3000 ms → payments is **Degraded** (> 1000 ms rule).
  - The timeout must also be less than the check interval (Better Stack's rule).
- **Q-C. X and N** for the failure ratio. Example: the drill's quotes runs at `flaky 50%`. The chosen X/N decides whether quotes shows Degraded, and whether random runs of 3 failures also push it to Down.
- **Q-D. Recovery from Degraded.** Do 2 successes in a row also clear Degraded, or must latency < 1000 ms and the failure ratio ≤ X both hold?
- **Q-E. Degraded → Down escalation.** If an incident is open for Degraded and the service then goes Down, do I **update the same incident** (raise its severity) or open a new one? *(Research suggests one open incident per service. Waiting on PO Q6.)*
- **Q-F. Notifications for degraded incidents.** Does a webhook fire on degraded-opened too, or only on down? Is there a webhook on severity change?
- **Q-G. Check interval.** Default and minimum allowed interval (PO Q1). Note: the `--fast` drill keeps claims down for only **40 s**, so with 3 failures needed, the interval must be **≤ ~10 s** for claims to be detected in time.
- **Q-H. Availability unit.** Measure by **check count** (ok checks / total) or by **time** (seconds in Down / window)? How should a service added mid-window, or periods with no data, be treated?

---

## 5. Scope

### Must-haves (build in this order) ✅
1. Service catalogue: API + UI (name, health URL, interval, timeout, owner, SLO target), with validation
2. Health checker: one async task per service, each with its own timeout; every result stored
3. Service state: a pure function for Healthy / Degraded / Down / recovery
4. Incidents: auto-open and auto-resolve; acknowledge; notes; timeline
5. Notifications: webhook on open and on resolve, with retry, every attempt logged
6. Operator dashboard
7. Public status page (no internal details)
8. Reliability: availability against target, error budget remaining
9. Product metrics
10. One-command run (docker compose) + README

*The order above is my proposal. To be adjusted after PO Q10.*

### Out of scope
⏳ **Not decided yet.** 💡 Candidates from research, for me to confirm or reject:
- Escalation policies and on-call rotations: a product in themselves; "acknowledged by" covers the must-have
- Status page subscriptions (email/SMS): need delivery, unsubscribe and abuse protection; listed as "going further"
- Maintenance windows: change the SLO maths; not required
- Non-HTTP checks and multi-region checks: the kit exposes HTTP `/health` only
- Operator login: depends on PO Q12
- Statuspage-style 4-stage public lifecycle and 5 status levels: need a person to write updates; 3 states are enough

---

## 6. System design

```
                       docker compose (one network)
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                   │
 │  ┌──────────────────────── Pulse (FastAPI) ─────────────────────┐ │
 │  │                                                              │ │
 │  │  Scheduler ── one asyncio task per service ──┐               │ │
 │  │      │  (own interval, own httpx timeout)    │ GET /health   │ │
 │  │      ▼                                       ▼               │ │
 │  │  check_results ──► State engine (pure fn) ──► Incident mgr   │ │
 │  │                         │                       │            │ │
 │  │                         ▼                       ▼            │ │
 │  │                    services.state        Notifier (retry) ───┼─┼──► webhook-receiver:9000
 │  │                                                              │ │
 │  │  Web: /dashboard  /services  /incidents/{id}  /metrics       │ │
 │  │       /status (public)   /api/...                            │ │
 │  │                                                              │ │
 │  │  SQLite file (volume)                                        │ │
 │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
 │                                                                   │
 │  quotes:8080   payments:8080   claims:8080   notifications:8080   │
 │  (starter kit, unchanged)                                         │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Isolation:** each service has its own task and its own timeout, so a slow service cannot delay the others.
- **State engine** is a pure function `(recent checks, current state, rules) → new state`. No I/O, so it is easy to test.
- **Catalogue changes** (add, edit, delete) start, restart or stop that service's task.
- Whether the SQLite file lives on a persistent volume depends on PO Q11 ⏳.

---

## 7. Data model (SQLite)

```
services
  id PK, name UNIQUE, health_url, interval_s, timeout_ms, owner,
  slo_target (e.g. 99.9), state (healthy|degraded|down|unknown),
  state_since, created_at, updated_at

check_results
  id PK, service_id FK, checked_at, scheduled_at,   -- scheduled_at → scheduler lag
  ok BOOL, status_code NULL, latency_ms NULL, error TEXT NULL  -- error is internal only
  INDEX (service_id, checked_at)

incidents
  id PK, service_id FK, severity (degraded|down),
  status (open|acknowledged|resolved),
  first_failure_at,       -- for MTTD
  opened_at, acknowledged_at NULL, acknowledged_by NULL, resolved_at NULL
  -- rule: at most one non-resolved incident per service (pending PO Q6)

incident_events            -- the timeline
  id PK, incident_id FK, at, type (opened|state_change|acknowledged|note|resolved|notified),
  actor NULL, message

notifications
  id PK, incident_id FK, event (opened|resolved), attempt, sent_at,
  http_status NULL, success BOOL, error NULL
```

---

## 8. Main screens

**Operator dashboard** `/dashboard`
```
┌ Pulse ─────────────────────────────────── auto-refresh ┐
│ OPEN INCIDENTS                                         │
```

# Pulse – Plan (Gate 1)

> Legend: **✅ Decided** · **⏳ TBD**: open, must be resolved before or while building · **💡 Proposal**: awaiting my confirmation

---

## 1. Problem in my words

Acko runs many services. When one fails or slows down, nobody finds out in time:

| User | Pain today | Outcome they need |
|---|---|---|
| **On-call engineers** (service owners) | Hear about failures late, often from support | Get alerted fast, with one incident per outage, a timeline, and the ability to acknowledge and add notes |
| **Support team** | Customers call and support has no context | See at a glance what is broken and since when |
| **Customers** | Payment fails or claim is stuck: "is it me or Acko?" | A public status page in plain language, with no internal details |
| **Leads** (secondary) | Can't say how reliable a service really was | Availability against target, and the error budget left |

**The outcome that matters:** detect problems quickly (low MTTD), don't cry wolf (no flapping or duplicate incidents), and keep everyone informed until recovery.

---

## 2. Product owner Q&A

| # | Question | PO answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How frequently should Pulse check each service? | ⏳ *awaiting answer* |
| 2 | What timeout should classify a service as slow or unhealthy? | ⏳ |
| 3 | Should one failed check create an incident, or multiple consecutive failures? | ⏳ |
| 4 | How many successful checks before resolving an incident? | ⏳ |
| 5 | What conditions classify degraded rather than down? | ⏳ |
| 6 | Can multiple incidents be open for the same service? | ⏳ |
| 7 | What exact payload and endpoint does the webhook receiver expect? | ⏳ |
| 8 | Should customers see detailed error messages or only service status? | ⏳ |
| 9 | What observation window for availability? | ⏳ |
| 10 | Which features matter most if I can't finish everything? | ⏳ |
| 11 | Should historical check data survive restarts? | ⏳ |
| 12 | Is authentication required for the operator dashboard? | ⏳ |

*Answers to be copied word for word. Where the PO says "your call", the decision goes in DECISIONS.md.*

---

## 3. Research findings (Statuspage, Uptime Kuma, Better Stack, PagerDuty, UptimeRobot)

- **Anti-flapping is standard.** Uptime Kuma uses retries and a "Pending" state before "Down". Better Stack uses a confirmation period before opening and a recovery period before resolving, and any failure resets recovery. → Supports my "3 failures in a row" and "2 successes in a row" rules.
- **Dedup.** In PagerDuty, an event for an already-open incident is appended to it, not opened as a new incident. Ack events for resolved incidents are discarded.
- **Lifecycle.** PagerDuty and Better Stack use Triggered/Open → Acknowledged → Resolved. Acknowledging stops escalation.
- **Notifications.** PagerDuty notifies on trigger by default. Statuspage SMS goes out only on create and resolve.
- **Public page.** Statuspage separates component status (Operational / Degraded Performance / Partial Outage / Major Outage / Maintenance) from internal detail.
- **Config validation.** Better Stack rejects a check interval shorter than the request timeout.
- **Metrics.** PagerDuty: MTTA = created → first ack; MTTR = created → resolved; open incidents are excluded.
- **SLO / error budget.** I found no native per-service SLO with error budget in the four tools I verified. Datadog has one. This is where Pulse adds value. Reference: 99.9% over 30 days = 43.2 min of budget.

---

## 4. Decisions so far

| Area | Decision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Stack | Python **FastAPI** + **SQLite** + **httpx** (async) + server-rendered HTML (Jinja2) + **pytest** | ✅ |
| Down rule | **3 failed checks in a row, or timeout** | ✅ (see open Q-A, Q-B) |
| Degraded rule | **Response > 1000 ms, or failure ratio > X in last N checks** | ✅ shape / ⏳ X and N |
| Recovery rule | **2 successful checks in a row** | ✅ (see open Q-D) |
| Incident opens on | **Down + Degraded** | ✅ (see open Q-E, Q-F) |
| SLO window | **Rolling 30 days**, plus a **1-hour view** for the demo | ✅ |
| Degraded counts as | ⏳ **up or down** in the availability calculation | ⏳ |
| Out of scope | ⏳ see §5 | ⏳ |

### Open questions arising from my rules (must be resolved)

- **Q-A. "Or timeout".** Does a **single** timeout mark the service Down immediately, or does a timeout count as **one failure** towards the 3-in-a-row?
- **Q-B. Timeout value.** Not decided. This matters for the drill: payments is set to `slow 3000ms` and **still returns 200**.
  - If timeout < 3000 ms → payments is treated as **Down**.
  - If timeout > 3000 ms → payments is **Degraded** (> 1000 ms rule).
  - The timeout must also be less than the check interval (Better Stack's rule).
- **Q-C. X and N** for the failure ratio. Example: the drill's quotes runs at `flaky 50%`. The chosen X/N decides whether quotes shows Degraded, and whether random runs of 3 failures also push it to Down.
- **Q-D. Recovery from Degraded.** Do 2 successes in a row also clear Degraded, or must latency < 1000 ms and the failure ratio ≤ X both hold?
- **Q-E. Degraded → Down escalation.** If an incident is open for Degraded and the service then goes Down, do I **update the same incident** (raise its severity) or open a new one? *(Research suggests one open incident per service. Waiting on PO Q6.)*
- **Q-F. Notifications for degraded incidents.** Does a webhook fire on degraded-opened too, or only on down? Is there a webhook on severity change?
- **Q-G. Check interval.** Default and minimum allowed interval (PO Q1). Note: the `--fast` drill keeps claims down for only **40 s**, so with 3 failures needed, the interval must be **≤ ~10 s** for claims to be detected in time.
- **Q-H. Availability unit.** Measure by **check count** (ok checks / total) or by **time** (seconds in Down / window)? How should a service added mid-window, or periods with no data, be treated?

---

## 5. Scope

### Must-haves (build in this order) ✅
1. Service catalogue: API + UI (name, health URL, interval, timeout, owner, SLO target), with validation
2. Health checker: one async task per service, each with its own timeout; every result stored
3. Service state: a pure function for Healthy / Degraded / Down / recovery
4. Incidents: auto-open and auto-resolve; acknowledge; notes; timeline
5. Notifications: webhook on open and on resolve, with retry, every attempt logged
6. Operator dashboard
7. Public status page (no internal details)
8. Reliability: availability against target, error budget remaining
9. Product metrics
10. One-command run (docker compose) + README

*The order above is my proposal. To be adjusted after PO Q10.*

### Out of scope
⏳ **Not decided yet.** 💡 Candidates from research, for me to confirm or reject:
- Escalation policies and on-call rotations: a product in themselves; "acknowledged by" covers the must-have
- Status page subscriptions (email/SMS): need delivery, unsubscribe and abuse protection; listed as "going further"
- Maintenance windows: change the SLO maths; not required
- Non-HTTP checks and multi-region checks: the kit exposes HTTP `/health` only
- Operator login: depends on PO Q12
- Statuspage-style 4-stage public lifecycle and 5 status levels: need a person to write updates; 3 states are enough

---

## 6. System design

```
                       docker compose (one network)
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                   │
 │  ┌──────────────────────── Pulse (FastAPI) ─────────────────────┐ │
 │  │                                                              │ │
 │  │  Scheduler ── one asyncio task per service ──┐               │ │
 │  │      │  (own interval, own httpx timeout)    │ GET /health   │ │
 │  │      ▼                                       ▼               │ │
 │  │  check_results ──► State engine (pure fn) ──► Incident mgr   │ │
 │  │                         │                       │            │ │
 │  │                         ▼                       ▼            │ │
 │  │                    services.state        Notifier (retry) ───┼─┼──► webhook-receiver:9000
 │  │                                                              │ │
 │  │  Web: /dashboard  /services  /incidents/{id}  /metrics       │ │
 │  │       /status (public)   /api/...                            │ │
 │  │                                                              │ │
 │  │  SQLite file (volume)                                        │ │
 │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
 │                                                                   │
 │  quotes:8080   payments:8080   claims:8080   notifications:8080   │
 │  (starter kit, unchanged)                                         │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Isolation:** each service has its own task and its own timeout, so a slow service cannot delay the others.
- **State engine** is a pure function `(recent checks, current state, rules) → new state`. No I/O, so it is easy to test.
- **Catalogue changes** (add, edit, delete) start, restart or stop that service's task.
- Whether the SQLite file lives on a persistent volume depends on PO Q11 ⏳.

---

## 7. Data model (SQLite)

```
services
  id PK, name UNIQUE, health_url, interval_s, timeout_ms, owner,
  slo_target (e.g. 99.9), state (healthy|degraded|down|unknown),
  state_since, created_at, updated_at

check_results
  id PK, service_id FK, checked_at, scheduled_at,   -- scheduled_at → scheduler lag
  ok BOOL, status_code NULL, latency_ms NULL, error TEXT NULL  -- error is internal only
  INDEX (service_id, checked_at)

incidents
  id PK, service_id FK, severity (degraded|down),
  status (open|acknowledged|resolved),
  first_failure_at,       -- for MTTD
  opened_at, acknowledged_at NULL, acknowledged_by NULL, resolved_at NULL
  -- rule: at most one non-resolved incident per service (pending PO Q6)

incident_events            -- the timeline
  id PK, incident_id FK, at, type (opened|state_change|acknowledged|note|resolved|notified),
  actor NULL, message

notifications
  id PK, incident_id FK, event (opened|resolved), attempt, sent_at,
  http_status NULL, success BOOL, error NULL
```

---

**Operator dashboard** `/dashboard`
```

│ payments     ● Degraded 3012 ms  ▁▁▇▇▇     99.90%  51%  │
│ claims       ● Down        –     ▁▁▁__     99.40%   0%  │
│ notifications● Healthy   38 ms   ▁▁▁▁▁    100.00% 100%  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ RECENT INCIDENTS (resolved)                  [all →]   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Catalogue changes** (add, edit, delete) start, restart or stop that service's task.
- Whether the SQLite file lives on a persistent volume depends on PO Q11 ⏳.

---

## 7. Data model (SQLite)

```
services
  id PK, name UNIQUE, health_url, interval_s, timeout_ms, owner,
  slo_target (e.g. 99.9), state (healthy|degraded|down|unknown),
  state_since, created_at, updated_at

check_results
  id PK, service_id FK, checked_at, scheduled_at,   -- scheduled_at → scheduler lag
  ok BOOL, status_code NULL, latency_ms NULL, error TEXT NULL  -- error is internal only
  INDEX (service_id, checked_at)

incidents
  id PK, service_id FK, severity (degraded|down),
  status (open|acknowledged|resolved),
  first_failure_at,       -- for MTTD
  opened_at, acknowledged_at NULL, acknowledged_by NULL, resolved_at NULL
  -- rule: at most one non-resolved incident per service (pending PO Q6)

incident_events            -- the timeline
  id PK, incident_id FK, at, type (opened|state_change|acknowledged|note|resolved|notified),
  actor NULL, message

notifications
  id PK, incident_id FK, event (opened|resolved), attempt, sent_at,
  http_status NULL, success BOOL, error NULL
```

---

## 8. Main screens

**Operator dashboard** `/dashboard`
```
┌ Pulse ─────────────────────────────────── auto-refresh ┐
│ OPEN INCIDENTS                                         │
│ ● claims   DOWN      since 14:02 (6m)  [Ack] [View]    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Service      State      Latency  Trend       30d  Budget left │
│ quotes       ● Healthy   42 ms   ▁▂▁▁▂     99.95%  80%  │
│ payments     ● Degraded 3012 ms  ▁▁▇▇▇     99.90%  51%  │
│ claims       ● Down        –     ▁▁▁__     99.40%   0%  │
│ notifications● Healthy   38 ms   ▁▁▁▁▁    100.00% 100%  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ RECENT INCIDENTS (resolved)                  [all →]   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Incident detail** `/incidents/{id}`
```
claims – DOWN – Acknowledged by <name>     duration 6m 12s
Timeline
 14:01:50  first failed check
 14:02:10  incident opened (3 consecutive failures)
 14:02:11  webhook sent: opened (200)
 14:03:00  acknowledged by <name>
 14:04:30  note: "DB failover in progress"
 14:08:02  resolved (2 consecutive successes)
[ Add note ______________ ] [Acknowledge]
```

**Public status page** `/status` (no owners, errors, IPs or notes)
```
Acko System Status            ● Some systems are affected
Payments         Degraded performance
Claims           Operational
Quotes           Operational
Notifications    Operational
History (last ⏳ N days): ▮▮▮▮▮▮▯▮▮▮ per service
Past incidents: "Claims – service disruption – resolved, 6 min"
```

**Catalogue** `/services`: a table plus an add/edit form (name, URL, interval, timeout, owner, target).

**Metrics** `/metrics` (HTML) and `/api/metrics` (JSON), see §10.

---

## 9. Test plan (pytest)

**Unit**
- State engine, table-driven:
  - healthy → down after 3 failures in a row
  - 1 or 2 failures do **not** go down
  - latency > 1000 ms → degraded
  - failure ratio > X in N → degraded (⏳ X, N)
  - 2 successes → recovered
  - a failure during recovery resets the count
  - flaky 50% does not flap open/close on every check
  - timeout behaviour per Q-A
- Availability and error budget: hand-computed examples, no data, service added mid-window, degraded counted per ⏳ decision
- Catalogue validation: unique name, target in (0, 100], timeout < interval, minimum interval (⏳ value)

**Integration**
- Catalogue CRUD API
- Scheduler isolation: one service set to 3 s slow, the others are still checked on schedule (measured through `scheduled_at` vs `checked_at`)
- Incidents: no duplicates under flapping; acknowledge after resolve is rejected; timeline is in order
- Notifier against the real webhook receiver (`GET /api/received`): exactly one "opened" and one "resolved"; retry when the receiver is down
- Public page: with a service down, the HTML must **not** contain `10.12.4.7`, `timeout`, `-db`, owner names or notes

**Acceptance**
- Script: start the stack, run `incident-drill.sh --fast`, then assert:
  - claims: exactly 1 incident opened and resolved
  - payments: state matches the rules (⏳ depends on Q-B)
  - quotes: behaviour matches the X/N rule
  - webhook count is as expected
  - the public page leaks nothing

---

## 10. Metrics (how I will know Pulse works)

| Metric | Definition |
|---|---|
| **MTTD** | `incident.opened_at − first_failure_at` |
| **MTTA** | `acknowledged_at − opened_at` (unacknowledged incidents excluded) |
| **MTTR** | `resolved_at − opened_at` (open incidents excluded) |
| Incident count | Per service, per window |
| Check success rate | ok / total checks |
| Check latency | p50 / p95 per service |
| **Scheduler lag** | `checked_at − scheduled_at`, p95 (shows Pulse's own health) |
| Webhook delivery | Success % and attempts per notification |
| Availability / budget | Per service against target (formula ⏳ Q-H) |

**Success criteria for the demo:**
- The drill produces the expected incidents, with no duplicates.
- Claims is detected within the `--fast` window.
- Scheduler lag stays under 1 s while payments is slow.
- 0 leaks on the public page.

1. How frequently should Pulse check each service?
Recommended answer: Every 10 seconds by default.
- Each service should have its own configurable check interval.
- Default interval: 10 seconds.
- Allow operators to configure it, for example, between 5 and 60 seconds.
- Checks should execute independently so one slow service doesn't delay others.
Why? A 10-second interval provides reasonably quick detection without generating excessive requests.
2. What timeout should classify a service as slow or unhealthy?
Recommended answer:
- Request timeout: 3 seconds.
- Healthy: HTTP 2xx response within 1 second.
- Degraded: HTTP 2xx response taking more than 1 second but less than 3 seconds.
- Failed: Non-2xx response, connection error or timeout.
Why? We need to distinguish a service that is responding slowly from one that is completely unavailable.
3. Should one failed check create an incident, or should multiple consecutive failures be required?
Recommended answer: Require two consecutive failed checks before marking a service DOWN and creating an incident.
- First failure: Mark the service as potentially unhealthy.
- Second consecutive failure: Mark it DOWN and automatically open an incident.
- Successful check between failures: Reset the consecutive failure counter.
Why? This reduces false-positive incidents caused by temporary network problems.
4. How many successful checks should be required before resolving an incident?
Recommended answer: Two consecutive successful checks.
- First successful check: Mark the service as recovering.
- Second consecutive successful check: Confirm recovery.
- Update the service status to HEALTHY and resolve the active incident.
Why? One successful response does not necessarily mean the service has fully recovered.
5. What conditions should classify a service as degraded rather than down?
Recommended answer:
Condition    Status
HTTP 2xx and response time ≤ 1 second    HEALTHY
HTTP 2xx and response time > 1 second but < 3 seconds    DEGRADED
One consecutive failed check    DEGRADED
Two consecutive failed checks    DOWN
Two consecutive successful checks after failure    HEALTHY


A service can be degraded without creating a critical incident.

Why? Degraded status helps operators identify performance problems before they become complete outages.
6. Can multiple incidents remain open for the same service?
Recommended answer: No, not for the same active outage.
- Allow only one unresolved incident per service.
- Additional failures should update the existing incident timeline.
- Once resolved, a new failure can create a new incident.
- Store acknowledgement and resolution timestamps.
Why? This prevents duplicate incident notifications and keeps incident history clean.
7. What exact payload and endpoint does the webhook receiver expect?
Recommended answer: First inspect the starter kit's README and webhook receiver source code. Do not invent the endpoint or payload.

For the proposed implementation, I would use an event structure like this, subject to the receiver's actual contract:
{
  "event": "incident.opened",
  "incident_id": "INC-001",
  "service": "payments",
  "status": "DOWN",
  "message": "Service health check failed",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"
}

For recovery:
{
  "event": "incident.resolved",
  "incident_id": "INC-001",
  "service": "payments",
  "status": "HEALTHY",
  "message": "Service recovered",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-18T12:05:00Z"
}

Use HTTP POST and JSON only if that matches the receiver's contract.

Why? Integrating with the provided webhook receiver is a required feature, so compatibility matters more than inventing a sophisticated payload.
8. Should customers see detailed error messages or only service status?
Recommended answer: Only service status and customer-friendly incident information.

Public page should show:
- Service name.
- Current status.
- Incident start time.
- Customer-friendly incident description.
- Recovery status.
- Recent incident history.
Do not expose:
- Internal stack traces.
- Database errors.
- Internal IP addresses.
- Sensitive infrastructure information.
Why? The public status page is designed to inform customers, not expose internal implementation details.
9. What observation window should be used to calculate availability?
Recommended answer: A rolling 24-hour window for the MVP, with an option to view seven-day history if time permits.

Formula:
\[
Availability = \frac{Successful\ Checks}{Total\ Eligible\ Checks} \times 100
\]
For example:
- Total eligible checks: 8,640.
- Successful checks: 8,553.
\[
Availability = \frac{8553}{8640}\times100
= 98.99\%
\]
Also calculate:
\[
Error\ Budget = Allowed\ Downtime - Observed\ Downtime
\]
For a 99.9% availability target over 24 hours:
\[
Allowed\ Downtime = 24 \times 60 \times 0.001
= 1.44\text{ minutes}
\]
Clearly distinguish measured data from missing historical data. Do not assume the service was healthy before monitoring began.
10. Which features matter most if I cannot complete everything in six hours?
Recommended answer: Prioritise the complete incident detection and recovery workflow.
Priority    Feature
P0    Service catalogue
P0    Scheduled health checks
P0    Healthy, degraded and down states
P0    Automatic incident creation
P0    Incident acknowledgement and resolution
P0    Public status page
P0    Webhook notifications
P1    Reliability and availability metrics
P1    Response-time history
P1    Incident timeline and notes
P2    Authentication
P2    Advanced analytics
P2    Customer subscriptions


Why? A smaller, working product with tested incident detection and recovery is better than a large unfinished product.
11. Should historical health-check data survive application restarts?
Recommended answer: Yes.

Store health-check results, incidents and incident events in PostgreSQL.
- Persist every health-check result.
- Preserve incident history.
- Restore active incidents when the application restarts.
- Resume scheduled checks after restart.
- Do not delete historical data when the backend restarts.
Why? Reliability tracking depends on historical data. In-memory storage would lose important information after a restart.
12. Is authentication required for the operator dashboard?
Recommended answer: For the six-hour MVP, authentication is not in the critical path unless the product owner explicitly requires it.
- Keep the operator dashboard as an internal/demo interface.
- Keep the public status page read-only.
- Do not expose internal incident details through public APIs.
- Document that production deployment requires authentication and role-based access control.
Why? Authentication is not listed among the Pulse must-haves. It is mentioned as a possible extension in the problem statement.     DevOps Intern Product Build – P…
Final decisions to put in your PLAN.md
Here is a concise decision table you can use:
Configuration    Decision
Default health-check interval    10 seconds
Request timeout    3 seconds
Slow response threshold    1 second
Failure threshold    2 consecutive failures
Recovery threshold    2 consecutive successes
Degraded state    Slow response or first consecutive failure
Duplicate active incidents    Not allowed per service
Availability window    Rolling 24 hours
Historical storage    PostgreSQL
Public information    Customer-friendly status only
Authentication    Deferred for MVP
Webhook    Follow provided receiver contract

# Pulse – Plan (Gate 1)

> Legend: **✅ Decided** (by me) · **⏳ Open**: to resolve while building, logged in DECISIONS.md · **💡 Proposal**: not yet confirmed

---

## 1. Problem in my words

Acko runs many services. When one fails or slows down, nobody finds out in time:

| User | Pain today | Outcome they need |
|---|---|---|
| **On-call engineers** (service owners) | Hear about failures late, often from support | A fast alert, one incident per outage, a timeline, acknowledge and notes |
| **Support team** | Customers call and support has no context | See at a glance what is broken and since when |
| **Customers** | Payment fails or claim is stuck: "is it me or Acko?" | A public status page in plain language, with no internal details |
| **Leads** (secondary) | Can't say how reliable a service really was | Availability against target, and the error budget left |

**The outcome that matters:** detect outages quickly, don't cry wolf (one incident per outage, no leaks), and keep everyone informed until recovery.

---

## 2. Product owner Q&A

The answers below are **my own working decisions**. The PO has not answered these yet. When the PO replies, I will copy the answers word for word into the last column, and log any change in DECISIONS.md.

| # | Question | My decision | PO answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How often should Pulse check each service? | Per-service interval, **default 10 s**, allowed **6–60 s**; checks independent | ⏳ not yet asked |
| 2 | What timeout makes a check slow or unhealthy? | **Timeout 5 s**. 2xx ≤ 1 s = good, 2xx > 1 s = slow, non-2xx / connection error / timeout = failed | ⏳ |
| 3 | Does one failed check create an incident? | No. **2 consecutive failures → DOWN + incident**. A success in between resets the count. | ⏳ |
| 4 | How many successes resolve an incident? | **2 consecutive successes** → HEALTHY, incident resolved | ⏳ |
| 5 | Degraded vs down? | **Degraded** = slow 2xx, or 1st failure. **Down** = 2 failures in a row. Degraded alone opens **no** incident. | ⏳ |
| 6 | Multiple open incidents per service? | **No.** At most 1 unresolved incident per service; further failures append to its timeline | ⏳ |
| 7 | Webhook endpoint and payload? | Receiver accepts **POST, any path, any JSON, always 200** (verified in `webhook-receiver/app.py`). Payload designed by me (§6) | ⏳ |
| 8 | Error details for customers? | **Status only**, plus customer-friendly incident text. No errors, IPs, hosts, owners or notes | ⏳ |
| 9 | Availability window? | **Rolling 24 h** (7 days if time allows). Check-based formula (§9) | ⏳ |
| 10 | Priorities if time runs out? | P0/P1/P2 list in §5 | ⏳ |
| 11 | Must history survive restarts? | **Yes.** SQLite on a Docker volume; active incidents and schedules resume after restart | ⏳ |
| 12 | Auth for the operator dashboard? | **Deferred** for the MVP; documented as needed in production | ⏳ |

---

## 3. Research findings (Statuspage, Uptime Kuma, Better Stack, PagerDuty, UptimeRobot)

- **Anti-flapping is standard.** Uptime Kuma puts a monitor in "Pending" and retries before "Down". Better Stack has a confirmation period before opening an incident and a recovery period before resolving, and any failure resets the recovery period. → I adopted 2 failures to open and 2 successes to resolve.
- **Dedup.** In PagerDuty, an event for an already-open incident is appended to it. Ack events for resolved incidents are discarded. → One open incident per service; acknowledging a resolved incident is rejected.
- **Lifecycle.** PagerDuty and Better Stack use Open → Acknowledged → Resolved. → Adopted.
- **Notifications.** PagerDuty notifies on trigger by default. Statuspage SMS goes out only on create and resolve. → Webhooks on opened and resolved only.
- **Public page.** Statuspage keeps component status separate from internal detail. → A fixed public vocabulary.
- **Config validation.** Better Stack rejects a check interval shorter than the timeout. → Validate timeout < interval.
- **Metrics.** PagerDuty: MTTA = created → first ack; MTTR = created → resolved; open incidents excluded. → Adopted, plus MTTD.
- **SLO / error budget.** I found no native per-service SLO with error budget in the four tools I verified. Datadog has one. This is Pulse's point of difference.

---

## 4. Decisions

| Area | Decision |
|---|---|
| Stack | Python **FastAPI** + **SQLite** (WAL mode, file on a Docker volume) + **httpx** async + Jinja2 server-rendered HTML + **pytest** |
| Interval | Default 10 s; validated range 6–60 s |
| Timeout | 5 s (must be < interval) |
| Slow threshold | 1000 ms |
| Healthy | 2xx within ≤ 1000 ms |
| Degraded | 2xx > 1000 ms, **or** first failure |
| Down | **2 consecutive failures** (non-2xx, connection error or timeout) |
| Recovery | **2 consecutive successes** → HEALTHY, incident resolved |
| Incident opens on | **DOWN only** |
| Duplicate incidents | Not allowed: 1 unresolved incident per service |
| Flaky services | **Accepted:** each separate outage opens its own incident. The dashboard shows the failure rate so flakiness is visible. |
| Availability | Rolling **24 h**, check-based; 7 days if time allows |
| Public page | Customer-friendly status only |
| Auth | Deferred for the MVP |
| Webhook | POST JSON to `http://webhook-receiver:9000/pulse` on opened and resolved |

**Changed from my earlier draft:**
- 3 failures → **2**: faster detection; claims in the `--fast` drill is down for only 40 s.
- Incidents on Down + Degraded → **Down only**: degraded is a warning, not an outage.
- 30-day window → **24 h**: a demo can produce meaningful 24 h numbers; 30 days would be almost empty.
- Considered PostgreSQL → kept **SQLite on a volume**: it meets the "survive restarts" requirement with less setup.
- Timeout 3 s → **5 s**: the drill's `slow 3000ms` returns 200 after ~3 s. With a 3 s timeout it would time out and show **Down**. With 5 s it correctly shows **Degraded**.

### How the drill should behave under these rules (predicted)

| Drill step | Expected Pulse behaviour |
|---|---|
| claims down (40 s fast / 120 s full) | DEGRADED after 1 check → DOWN + incident + webhook after the 2nd (≤ ~20 s) → resolved + webhook after 2 successes on reset |
| payments slow 3 s | DEGRADED, **no incident**, no webhook; back to HEALTHY on reset |
| quotes flaky 50% | Alternates HEALTHY/DEGRADED; **possibly 0..several incidents** (random). The acceptance test asserts consistency, not an exact count. |

### Open questions (decide while building, log in DECISIONS.md)

- **O-1. Slow responses and recovery.** Does a slow 2xx (> 1 s) count as a *success* for the 2-successes recovery rule? It does reset the failure counter. If so, does the service recover to DEGRADED rather than HEALTHY?
- **O-2. Display while recovering.** After the 1st success following DOWN, does the service show "DOWN (recovering)" or DEGRADED? The incident stays open either way.
- **O-3. Availability and slow checks.** Does a slow 2xx count as a successful check in the availability formula?
- **O-4. Error budget units.** Availability is check-based, but the budget is in minutes. Convert as `budget used = failed checks × interval`, or `minutes spent in DOWN`?
- **O-5. A service edited mid-window.** If its interval changes, does it affect the "eligible checks" count?
- **O-6. Webhook path and retries.** Path name (`/pulse` proposed). Retry count and backoff (proposed: 3 attempts, 1/2/4 s).
- **O-7. Out-of-scope candidates** (§5): confirm or reject.

---

## 5. Scope

### Build order (by priority)

| Priority | Feature | Must-have # |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | Service catalogue: API + UI, with validation | 1 |
| P0 | Scheduled health checks (one task per service, every result stored) | 2 |
| P0 | Healthy / Degraded / Down state engine | 3 |
| P0 | Automatic incident open / resolve; acknowledge | 4 |
| P0 | Public status page | 7 |
| P0 | Webhook notifications | 8 |
| P0 | One-command run + README | 10 |
| P1 | Incident timeline and notes | 4 ⚠️ |
| P1 | Reliability: availability + error budget | 5 |
| P1 | Response-time history, operator dashboard | 6 |
| P1 | Product metrics | 9 |
| P2 | Auth, advanced analytics, customer subscriptions | — |

⚠️ Timeline and notes are listed as P1 in my priorities, but **all of must-haves 1–10 are required** for a complete product. P1 means "build second", not "optional". Only P2 items are cut.

### Out of scope

- ✅ **Authentication / RBAC:** not a must-have; listed under "going further". Documented as needed in production.
- ✅ **Customer subscriptions:** need delivery, unsubscribe and abuse protection.
- ✅ **Advanced analytics:** beyond must-have #9.
- 💡 Escalation policies and on-call rotations: a product in themselves.
- 💡 Maintenance windows: would complicate the SLO maths.
- 💡 Non-HTTP and multi-region checks: the kit only exposes HTTP `/health`.

---

## 6. System design

```
                         docker compose (one network)
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  ┌─────────────────────────── Pulse (FastAPI) ───────────────────┐ │
 │  │                                                               │ │
 │  │  Scheduler: one asyncio task per service ──── GET /health ────┼─┼─► quotes / payments /
 │  │   (own interval, httpx timeout 5 s)                           │ │   claims / notifications
 │  │        │                                                      │ │   (kit, unchanged, :8080)
 │  │        ▼                                                      │ │
 │  │  check_results ─► State engine (PURE fn) ─► Incident manager  │ │
 │  │                      │                          │             │ │
 │  │                      ▼                          ▼             │ │
 │  │                 services.state            Notifier (retry) ───┼─┼─► webhook-receiver:9000/pulse
 │  │                                                               │ │
 │  │  Operator: /  /services  /incidents/{id}  /metrics            │ │
 │  │  Public:   /status        API: /api/...                       │ │
 │  │                                                               │ │
 │  │  SQLite (WAL) on volume pulse-data                            │ │
 │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Isolation:** a separate task and timeout per service, so a slow service never delays the others. Measured through scheduler lag.
- **State engine:** `next_state(current_state, counters, check) → (new_state, counters, events)`. No I/O, so it is fully table-testable.
- **Restart:** on startup, rebuild the consecutive-failure and success counters from the latest checks, reload open incidents, and restart every task.
- **Catalogue changes** start, restart or stop that service's task.
- **Webhook payload** (internal error text is never included):
  ```json
  {"event": "incident.opened", "incident_id": "INC-001", "service": "payments",
   "owner": "...", "status": "DOWN", "message": "Service health check failed",
   "timestamp": "2026-11-18T12:00:00Z"}
  ```
  `incident.resolved` has the same shape, with `"status": "HEALTHY"`, `"message": "Service recovered"`, and a `duration_s` field.
- **Retry testing:** the receiver always returns 200, so retries are tested by stopping the receiver container, or with a mock in unit tests.

---

## 7. Data model (SQLite)

```
services
  id PK, name UNIQUE, health_url, interval_s (6–60), timeout_ms (< interval),
  owner, slo_target (0–100, e.g. 99.9),
  state (unknown|healthy|degraded|down), state_since,
  consec_failures, consec_successes, created_at, updated_at

check_results
  id PK, service_id FK, scheduled_at, checked_at,   -- lag = checked_at − scheduled_at
  ok BOOL, slow BOOL, status_code NULL, latency_ms NULL,
  error TEXT NULL                                   -- internal only, never rendered publicly
  INDEX (service_id, checked_at)

incidents
  id PK, code ("INC-001"), service_id FK,
  status (open|acknowledged|resolved),
  first_failure_at,                                 -- for MTTD
  opened_at, acknowledged_at NULL, acknowledged_by NULL, resolved_at NULL,
  public_message                                    -- customer-friendly text
  -- rule: at most 1 row per service with status != resolved (enforced in code + partial unique index)

incident_events                                     -- timeline
  id PK, incident_id FK, at,
  type (opened|failure|acknowledged|note|recovering|resolved|notified),
  actor NULL, message

notifications
  id PK, incident_id FK, event (opened|resolved), attempt, sent_at,
  http_status NULL, success BOOL, error NULL
```

---

## 8. Main screens

**Operator dashboard** `/`
```
┌ Pulse – Operator ──────────────────────────── refreshes every 5 s ┐
│ OPEN INCIDENTS                                                    │
│ ● INC-003 claims   DOWN  since 14:02 (6m)   unacked   [Ack] [View]│
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Service       State      Latency  Last 20     Fail%  24h     Budget│
│ quotes        ● Degraded   41 ms  ▁▂✕▁✕▂✕    45%   99.31%   0.0m │
│ payments      ● Degraded 3012 ms  ▁▁▇▇▇▇▇     0%   100.0%   1.4m │
│ claims        ● Down         –    ▁▁✕✕✕✕✕   100%   98.90%   0.0m │
│ notifications ● Healthy    38 ms  ▁▁▁▁▁▁▁     0%   100.0%   1.4m │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ RECENT INCIDENTS  INC-002 quotes 40s resolved · INC-001 ...  [all]│
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Incident detail** `/incidents/{id}`
```
INC-003 · claims · DOWN · Acknowledged by <name> · open 6m 12s
Timeline
 14:01:50  check failed (503)                      ← first_failure_at
 14:02:00  incident opened (2 consecutive failures)
 14:02:01  webhook incident.opened → 200
 14:03:00  acknowledged by <name>
 14:04:30  note: "DB failover in progress"
 14:08:00  recovering (1/2 successes)
 14:08:10  resolved (2 consecutive successes) · webhook → 200
[ note ________________ ] [Add note] [Acknowledge]
```

**Public status page** `/status` (no owners, errors, IPs, notes or latencies)
```
Acko System Status                  ● Some systems are affected
Claims          ● Major outage        since 14:02
Payments        ● Degraded performance
Quotes          ● Operational
Notifications   ● Operational
Last 24 h:  claims ▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▯▯▮▮   (✅ up / ▯ down / grey = no data)
Recent incidents: "Claims – service disruption – resolved after 6 min"
```

**Catalogue** `/services`: a table plus an add/edit form (name, URL, interval, timeout, owner, target), with validation errors shown inline.

**Metrics** `/metrics` (HTML) and `/api/metrics` (JSON), see §10.

---

## 9. Reliability formula

- **Availability (24 h)** = successful checks ÷ eligible checks × 100.
  - Eligible = checks actually performed in the window. Time before monitoring began is **not** assumed healthy; it is shown as "no data".
  - Whether slow checks count as successful: ⏳ O-3.
- **Allowed downtime** = window minutes × (1 − target). For 99.9% over 24 h: **1.44 min**.
- **Budget remaining** = allowed − observed downtime (unit ⏳ O-4), shown in minutes and %. It can go negative, shown as "exhausted".
- *Note:* at 99.9% / 24 h, a single 20 s outage uses about 23% of the budget, so the drill will visibly exhaust it. That is good for the demo.

---

## 10. Test plan (pytest)

**Unit**
- State engine, table-driven:
  - 2xx ≤ 1 s → HEALTHY
  - 2xx > 1 s → DEGRADED
  - 1 failure → DEGRADED, no incident
  - 2 failures in a row → DOWN + open
  - F, S, F → never DOWN (the counter resets)
  - DOWN, S → still open (recovering); DOWN, S, S → HEALTHY + resolve
  - DOWN, S, F → stays DOWN, no new incident
  - timeout → failure
  - O-1 cases once decided
- Incidents:
  - a second DOWN while one is open → no new incident, timeline event added
  - ack on a resolved incident → rejected
  - acknowledging twice is idempotent
- Availability and budget:
  - hand-computed (8553 / 8640 = 98.99%)
  - no data → "no data", not 100%
  - a service added mid-window
  - budget exhausted shows as negative
- Catalogue validation: unique name, interval within 6–60, timeout < interval, target within (0, 100]
- Public view model: contains only whitelisted fields

**Integration**
- Catalogue CRUD via the API (FastAPI TestClient, temp SQLite)
- **Scheduler isolation:** one stub service delaying 4 s; the others' scheduler lag stays < 1 s
- Restart: create an open incident, restart the app → the incident is still open, counters are restored, checks resume
- Notifier: exactly 1 opened + 1 resolved per incident against the real receiver (`GET /api/received`); retry when the receiver is unreachable; every attempt recorded
- **Leak test:** with a service down, the `/status` HTML and the webhook bodies do **not** contain `10.12.4.7`, `timeout`, `-db`, owner names or note text

**Acceptance**
- Script: `docker compose up`, `DELETE /api/received`, run `incident-drill.sh --fast`, then assert:
  - claims: exactly 1 incident, opened and resolved, with 2 matching webhooks
  - payments: was DEGRADED, 0 incidents
  - quotes: every incident opened has been resolved, and webhooks = 2 × its incidents
  - all services HEALTHY at the end
  - `/status` has no leaks

---

## 11. Metrics (how I will know Pulse works)

| Metric | Definition | Target |
|---|---|---|
| **MTTD** | `opened_at − first_failure_at` | ≤ 1 interval (~10 s) |
| **MTTA** | `acknowledged_at − opened_at` (unacknowledged excluded) | shown |
| **MTTR** | `resolved_at − opened_at` (open excluded) | shown |
| Incidents | count per service, last 24 h | shown |
| Check success rate | ok ÷ total, per service | shown |
| Check latency | p50 / p95 per service | shown |
| **Scheduler lag** | p95 of `checked_at − scheduled_at` | < 1 s even while payments is slow |
| Webhook delivery | success %, average attempts | 100% eventually delivered |
| Public leaks | leak-test result | 0 |

**Demo success criteria:**
- The `--fast` drill produces exactly the predicted claims and payments behaviour.
- No duplicate incidents.
- Scheduler lag stays under 1 s.
- Zero leaks on the public page and in webhooks.

### Build order (by priority)

| Priority | Feature | Must-have # |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | Service catalogue: API + UI, with validation | 1 |
| P0 | Scheduled health checks (one task per service, every result stored) | 2 |

| P0 | Public status page | 7 |
| P0 | Webhook notifications | 8 |

| P1 | Incident timeline and notes | 4 ⚠️ |
| P1 | Reliability: availability + error budget | 5 |
| P1 | Response-time history, operator dashboard | 6 |
| P1 | Product metrics | 9 |
| P2 | Auth, advanced analytics, customer subscriptions | — |

- ✅ **Customer subscriptions:** need delivery, unsubscribe and abuse protection.
- ✅ **Advanced analytics:** beyond must-have #9.

- 💡 Maintenance windows: would complicate the SLO maths.

## 6. System design

